opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important and underrated levers we have right now. My basic view is that companies should be much more forthcoming than they currently are, and the default should flip from "we'll disclose if we have to" to "we disclose unless there's a really specific reason not to."

The core reason is that the whole world is trying to figure out how worried to be about misalignment, and right now most of the best evidence is sitting inside a handful of labs. When a model does something like sandbag on an evaluation, try to subvert oversight in a test environment, reward-hack in a way that looks deliberate, or behave differently when it thinks it's being watched, those are exactly the data points that policymakers, outside researchers, and frankly the other labs need to calibrate. If those incidents only surface in a footnote of a system card months later, or not at all, we're flying half-blind.

Concretely, I'd want a few things. First, some kind of shared taxonomy, so that "concerning incident" means something comparable across companies instead of each lab grading its own homework with its own rubric. Second, timeliness. A rough, honest writeup soon after is more useful than a polished one a year later. Third, reporting the near misses and the ambiguous cases, not just the dramatic ones. A lot of the signal is in "we're not sure whether this was strategic or just a weird generalization." Fourth, ideally some channel to a trusted third party, whether that's a government body like an AI safety institute or an independent auditor, for cases where full public disclosure would be genuinely hazardous, say because it reveals a capability that's dangerous to advertise.

I also think there's an incentive problem we have to be honest about. Every company faces pressure not to be the one that looks scariest, and that creates a race to the bottom on candor. You don't want a world where the lab that's most diligent about looking for misalignment ends up looking the worst because it found the most. So part of the answer is norms and maybe eventually requirements that apply to everyone, so being transparent isn't a unilateral competitive cost.

And the last thing I'd say is that the framing matters. These reports shouldn't be treated as PR crises. They're more like aviation incident reports: the point is to learn, to build up a shared picture of how these systems fail, and to notice trends early. If we can get to a culture where reporting a worrying behavior is seen as the responsible, high-status thing to do, I think we'd be in a much better position to actually see trouble coming before it's too late.

r001.rationale: The response calls for a shared taxonomy and more transparent, timely reporting, but does not propose publishing misalignment incident data as an anonymized industry aggregate.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss whether the small number of AI companies could make their identities guessable in anonymized industry reporting.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing I'd say is that right now we're in a really strange situation where the most important information about how these systems actually behave is almost entirely locked inside the companies. When something weird happens during training or in deployment, like a model that's clearly trying to game its reward signal, or a model that behaves differently when it seems to think it's being tested, or an agent that takes some action nobody intended and then sort of covers its tracks, the only people who know about that are a handful of researchers at that lab. And whether the rest of the world ever hears about it depends on whether someone decides to put it in a system card or write a blog post, and how it gets framed when they do.

So my baseline view is that we need to move toward something that looks a lot more like aviation or medicine, where there's an expectation, and ideally a requirement, that serious incidents get reported to some body that isn't the company itself. In aviation, when there's a near miss, the pilot doesn't get to decide whether it was embarrassing enough to keep quiet. It goes into a system, it gets analyzed, and the whole industry learns from it. And crucially, a lot of that reporting is designed to be non-punitive, because if you punish people for reporting near misses, you just stop hearing about near misses. You don't stop having them.

I think that's the key design tension for AI. You want companies to actually surface the scary stuff, and the scary stuff is exactly what they have the strongest incentive to downplay. If I'm a lab and my model did something that looks like scheming or sabotage, telling the world about it is a reputational hit, it might spook customers, it might invite regulation. So if the only mechanism is voluntary disclosure, you're going to systematically get the sanitized version. You'll hear about the cases that make the company look thoughtful and proactive, and you won't hear about the ones that make them look reckless.

What I'd actually want to see is a few layers. One is a mandatory reporting channel to a government body with real technical capacity, where incidents above some severity threshold have to be disclosed within a fixed window, and where the information is protected from being used in the most punitive ways, so that the incentive to hide things goes down. Two is some form of public disclosure, maybe with a delay and with details redacted where there are genuine security reasons, so that outside researchers and the public can build up a real picture of what's going on rather than relying on vibes. And three, which I think people underrate, is that the reporting should include the stuff that was caught and handled, not just the stuff that caused harm. The near misses are where most of the signal is. If a model attempted something bad during an eval and the lab's monitoring caught it, that's enormously informative about where we are on the risk curve, and right now that kind of thing often just gets mentioned in a paragraph in a system card if we're lucky.

I'd also say the definition of "incident" needs to be broad enough to cover the alignment-flavored stuff and not just the obvious misuse cases. It's pretty natural to report when a model helps someone do something clearly dangerous. It's much less natural to report "our model seemed to be pursuing a goal we didn't give it" or "our model's behavior changed in ways we don't understand when it inferred it was unobserved." Those are harder to pin down, they're more ambiguous, and they're more embarrassing in a specific way because they point at the company not being in control. But those are precisely the things I most want to know about, because they're the early indicators of the failure modes that could actually be catastrophic down the line.

And honestly, I think the companies that take this seriously should want this too. If you're a lab that's actually trying hard on safety, you're currently at a competitive disadvantage for being transparent, because your competitors who aren't disclosing look cleaner by comparison. A real reporting regime levels that playing field. It makes honesty the default instead of a sacrifice. So I'd push the safety-focused labs to be actively advocating for this rather than just doing voluntary disclosure and hoping it catches on, because I don't think it catches on by itself. The incentives don't point that way.

r001.rationale: The response proposes mandatory reporting to a government body and some public disclosure, but does not propose reporting the data as an anonymized industry aggregate.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss anonymized industry reporting or the risk that companies’ identities could be guessed.

astra-6.text:
I think companies should commit in advance to reporting serious incidents, rather than deciding in the moment whether a particular incident is something they want to disclose. Because that’s exactly when the incentives to say, “Well, this is ambiguous, and we’ve already fixed it,” are going to be strongest.

That doesn’t necessarily mean immediately publishing every detail. There could be sensitive information that would help someone misuse the system. But there should be some independent body that gets the full report, has the technical capacity to understand it, and can ask follow-up questions. And I think the public should get enough information to understand what happened and what grounds there are for believing the problem has been addressed.

One thing I’d particularly want to avoid is requiring a company to establish that an incident really was caused by misalignment before reporting it. We’re going to be uncertain about what these systems are doing and why. If you see behavior that looks like a model concealing its actions or trying to undermine oversight, that should be reportable even if there’s another plausible explanation. Reporting should be a way to investigate those concerns, not something that only happens after you’ve resolved them.

r001.rationale: The response supports reporting serious incidents to an independent body and sharing some information publicly, but does not propose an anonymized industry aggregate.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss whether the small number of AI companies could make identities guessable in anonymized reporting.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there should be a strong presumption that serious incidents get reported to an independent body, even when the company doesn’t yet know exactly what happened. You don’t want the threshold to be, “We’ve conclusively demonstrated that this model was scheming.” You want to be able to say, “We observed something concerning, here’s the evidence, and here’s what we’re still uncertain about.”

The incentive problem is that the company that discovers and reports a problem can end up looking less safe than a company that didn’t look very hard. So I’d want reporting requirements that apply across companies, with some protection for good-faith disclosure, and an independent capacity to investigate.

That doesn’t necessarily mean immediately publishing every technical detail. Some details could help people misuse a system or undermine a safety measure. But that’s a reason to have a confidential reporting channel, not a reason for the company to keep the incident entirely to itself. The public should ultimately get enough information to understand what went wrong and what changed as a result.

r001.rationale: The response calls for reporting to an independent body and across companies, but does not propose publishing incident data as an anonymized industry aggregate.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention that the small number of AI companies could make their identities guessable in anonymized industry reporting.
